item.title: UN’s COP31 Climate Conference Fizzles Out as Global Policy Divides Deepen
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: comprehensive coverage, clear prose, and valuable context

ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.

As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.

Many countries were not buying it.

For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.

The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.

The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.

Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.

In 2022, the U.N. conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.

Since then, international collaboration on climate issues has declined amid increased conflict, rising oil and gas prices and economic insecurity. The talks in Turkey ran two days beyond the scheduled end without reaching broad agreement on potential next steps, an outcome that won’t kill the global effort but is widely viewed as a serious setback.

But compromise for the sake of consensus is not enough, said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of the Environment.

“We will not be forced to accept false solutions,” she said. “We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.” As written, she added, the Antalya Pact undermines her country’s security and threatens its future.

“People are dying, seas are rising and ecosystems are collapsing,” Jetn̄il-Kijiner said. “Are we so divorced from reality that we take backward steps, even as overshoot threatens to overtake us? To accept this deal would be a betrayal to the Marshallese people.”

It’s not the first time Pacific Island nations threatened by rising seas have objected to the outcome at one of the United Nations’ annual conferences. During the 2023 U.N. talks in Dubai, a final text was adopted even though a delegation representing 39 small island developing states objected because they were still outside the plenary meeting, trying to coordinate their position.

But in Antalya, the divide ran much deeper. The economically powerful and politically influential European Union, representing 28 member countries, also rejected the proposed agreement.

Ireland’s climate, energy and environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the European countries formally objected to the cover decision because it fell short of what the global climate crisis demands.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the key driver of climate change, and not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” said O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU during Ireland’s rotating presidency.

Egypt and Brazil, hosts of the U.N. climate talks in 2023 and 2025, also criticized the text proposed by COP31 president Kurum of Turkey and Chris Bowen of Australia, president of the conference negotiations.

Liliam Beatris Chagas de Moura, director for climate at Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said she was disappointed that this year’s conference did not sustain the momentum from last year’s talks in her country.

Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator with the Saudi Arabian energy ministry, said the 22-member League of Arab States supported the proposed Antalya Pact. He criticized developed countries for using up most of the global carbon budget, the amount of fossil fuels that can be burned without overheating the planet, and then asking developing countries to give up the very energy sources that fueled their own growth.

Ayoub condemned some countries’ opposition to including references to carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture and storage in the pact, calling their resistance to those technologies unscientific.

Carbon capture and storage are not close to being deployed fast enough “to keep 1.5 degrees within reach,” he said, referring to the long-term goal of limiting the average global temperature increase established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table, and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances.”

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed” that the talks ended without consensus on an overarching agreement.…

item.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: strong analysis, clear argument, and useful vocabulary

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

Governments have spent the past 35 years negotiating the global response to preventing “dangerous interference” with the climate system. Over that same period global warming has increased to close to 1.4C, with observed warming now accelerating above 0.3C per decade. Now, we’re facing an imminent breach of the Paris agreement’s critical 1.5C warming limit.

Successive Australian governments have either actively denied the problem exists – or have talked loud and long about how they are playing their role.

And what a role it has been! Australia’s coal exports have tripled since 1991; LNG exports have increased 20-fold. Australia now contributes about 4.3% of global fossil carbon emissions through both its domestic activities, and as the third-largest exporter of fossil fuels of all time.

Now that Australia’s efforts to host successful climate talks have failed so badly to deliver at a global level, we must turn to the urgent question: what will the government deliver for Australians at home?

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has called the current decade “critical” for combating climate change. He told leaders at Cop31 they had a “solemn responsibility” to act – and he’s said that every fraction of a degree of warming prevented matters.

If anyone needed confirmation of that during the past year, they only needed to turn on the TV news or, in some cases, to walk out of their house. From Adelaide to Sydney, the south-east broiled in January. Bush burned, homes ignited, lungs filled with smoke. Can you guess what made the heat so brutal? And the floods so powerful?

Further afield, in countries that gave the Australian colony many of its people, things were equally desperate. Italy, Greece, Britain, Spain … all of Europe crackled through its summer, leaving an estimated 50,000 people dead before their time.

South and east Asia (many of them our LNG markets) shared the pain, with temperatures hitting a close-to-unliveable 52C in Pakistan. All of it driven by climate change; all of it driven by burning fossil fuels.

So that’s the logical framing when you hear government ministers from the prime minister down celebrating new fossil fuel finds, talking about how the country benefits from extracting and exporting coal, oil and gas.

What we’re exporting is climate pain.

The government clearly didn’t turn on the TV news nor leave its house this year: it was too busy planning for coal and gas exports staying close to present levels over the next decade, at exactly the time emissions globally should be halving.

In Australia’s approvals pipeline are four “carbon bombs”, defined by scientists as projects that could emit a billion or more tonnes of fossil CO2. Off the coast of Western Australia there’s the Browse gas development at the pristine Scott Reef, the Valhalla fracking project in WA’s Kimberley further north, the Beetaloo basin fracking project in the Northern Territory, and the massive Hunter Valley Operations coalmine in New South Wales.

Albanese’s ministers have shown little other than full-blooded support for these projects going ahead. Is it no wonder then that we left Antalya with no agreement?

Rather than a decision to build on the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) roadmap initiated by Brazil, the only reference to fossil fuels remaining in the final text offered by Turkey was the industry’s favoured get-out-of jail-free technology – carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS).

The Australian government has already thrown its weight behind CCS, including special legislation to allow for offshore CO2 disposal, with virtually no evidence of its effectiveness. It is an open secret that the world’s biggest CCS project at Chevron’s Gorgon project has spectacularly failed to deliver but this has not stopped the government backing this failed technology.

We couldn’t even see the call for 35% electrification by 2035 be “clean” even with science clearly showing that if it’s not clean it will increase fossil gas use – adding a tenth of a degree of warming by mid-century.

Indeed, while the prime minister says every tenth of a degree of warming matters, his problem is that lowering every tenth of a degree of warming means his beloved gas industry loses more market share.

This week the WA premier, Roger Cook, jets off to Japan with gas giant Woodside – to talk up LNG markets.

It’s unlikely he’s going there to tell the LNG industry what’s needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

It’s also unlikely he’ll mention the International Energy Agency’s report last week showing that to limit warming to 1.5C, fossil gas demand falls by about 40% from 2025 levels by 2035, driven by rapid electrification of end-uses, efficiency improvements, and the displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables.

Australians are looking to their federal and state governments to protect them from the terrifying ravages of climate change, yet those governments’ actions appear hyper-focused on fuelling more of it. And co-hosting the climate talks clearly didn’t help.

The government says it’s serious about climate action. By their fruits ye shall know them.

- Bill Hare, a physicist and climate scientist, is the chief executive of Climate Analytics

Source: The Guardian Environment | Published: 2026-11-22 22:30 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

EU officials reject Cop31 deal as it 'doesn't speak to reality of the climate crisis' – video

The Cop31 climate talks fell into disarray as the EU, UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate. Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, said the EU could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The president of the negotiations, Australia's Chris Bowen, called the failure 'very disappointing', saying that a lot of good work had been done but 'many parties who were people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts … those red lines on behalf of different parties were just not able to be met'.

item.title: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: topic is relevant but lacks depth and detail

On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

Wilson is among a group of prisoners who filed a lawsuit against the Florida department of corrections in 2024 for the conditions at the Dade correctional institution, alleging that the extreme heat contributed to four deaths and has subjected prisoners to cruel and unusual punishment. The bench trial began on Monday at a federal courthouse in downtown Miami serving the US district court for the southern district of Florida. The case comes amid growing concern over extreme heat in US prisons, where more than 40 states lack statewide policies requiring prisons to provide air conditioning, even as the climate crisis drives up summer temperatures and increases the risks.

Gary Wheeler, 67, who was also housed in the H dorms at the Dade correctional institute, testified that just months ago he thought he was having a heart attack, but upon going to the medical clinic in the prison he was told by a nurse that he had heat exhaustion. “I am worried about dying. I feel like sometimes when I go to sleep at night I’m not going to wake up in the morning,” he said. “My biggest fear is if I have a heatstroke and I can’t take care of myself, I have to depend on predators who could prey on you because you’re disabled.”

Both Wheeler and Wilson submitted informal grievances to the prison about the heat in the H dorms, some dating back to at least 2019. The men talked about another inmate affected by the heat named James “Jim” Beam, who was 83 years old, wheelchair bound, and had a respiratory condition. “He would breathe like he was gasping for air,” Wheeler said. “Every time he’d breathe he would throw his head back.”

Wilson said one night he woke up when he heard Beam hollering for help from his cell across the hall from him. “It was like 2am to 3am in the morning. He was on the floor,” Wilson said. Wilson helped Beam back into his wheelchair and brought him to the medical clinic, where he was put on a breathing treatment. But a doctor ended Beam’s treatment after about 30 minutes, after which Wilson pushed him back to his cell, he said. “The vent wasn’t working in the dorm. Jim’s tongue was kind of hanging out of his mouth and he was having problems breathing,” Wilson said. Within days, Beam died.

A medical examiner’s report found Beam’s death was caused by pneumonia, but Dr Susi Vassallo, an emergency medicine physician and medical toxicologist who has served as an expert witness in several cases involving heat in US prisons, testified that she believed long-term exposure to extreme heat contributed to his death, as well as the deaths of three other prisoners at the Dade correctional institute. Vassallo said that in no other case that she has participated in has there been such extensive heat data inside the prison. “It’s rather shocking, honestly,” she said of the temperatures and humidity levels captured by the sensors in the summer of 2025. “These are dangerous heat indices, putting these individuals at substantial risk of serious harm.”

In September, a US district court judge ruled that Texas must install air conditioning in all state prisons by the end of 2029. In that case, Vassallo had testified that air conditioning was the only way to reduce the heat and related risks of illnesses and deaths.

As rain pummeled the Miami courthouse on Wednesday, Vassallo said age, certain medical conditions and specific medicines can increase the risk of heat illnesses.

During their cross-examination of expert witnesses, attorneys for the Dade correctional institute argued that more than 100 ceiling and exhaust fans throughout the facility helped mitigate heat in the prison and that the eighth amendment prohibiting “cruel and unusual punishments” was not relevant. “In 1791, when the eighth amendment was ratified, there was no air conditioning,” said Mathew Gutierrez, defense counsel for the Florida department of corrections, FDC secretary Ricky Dixon and Dade correctional institution warden Francisco Acosta, in his opening statement on Monday. “So the lack of air conditioning could not have been encompassed in the eighth amendment.” Attorneys for the defendants also said that prisoners were permitted to wear shorts and had access to water jugs with ice during the summers. But prisoners said ice in the orange water coolers quickly melted because they were filled with hot water from the showers. Vassallo said that when temperatures reach a certain point, fans aren’t helpful, and they can actually increase body temperature.…
